changesets.summary: Add `leptoskit_query`, TanStack Query for leptos
changesets.details:
A new crate for async state management built on leptos's fine-grained signals: cached, deduplicated, retrying queries with stale-while-revalidate semantics, infinite queries that page in either direction, and mutations with lifecycle callbacks and optimistic updates. Queries refetch on window focus, reconnect, and interval; pause while offline; garbage collect when unobserved; and can stream server-fetched data to the browser through the same hydration mechanism leptos resources use.

Caches sync across browser tabs over a `BroadcastChannel`, or across the windows of a native app over any `BroadcastTransport`. Browser integration sits behind a default `browser` feature, so a wasm bundle hosted outside a browser — an iOS or Android shell — builds without it and installs its own clock and timer. The `leptoskit` meta crate re-exports it behind the `query` feature.

changesets.summary: Harden code push and layout; add the logo and docs
changesets.details:
Code push now rejects bundle paths that escape the staging directory, bounds decompression and delta output before allocating, refuses to overwrite a published release, writes releases atomically, offers deltas only against the exact release they were computed from, and falls back to the full download when a delta fails.

The layout engine caches measurements per node, so layout cost no longer grows exponentially with nesting depth. Flex free space, percentage bases, reversed axes, single-line `align-content`, grid placement of partly-auto items, grid row sizing, `minmax` growth, and `display: contents` in grid now follow CSS. Tree cycles and huge grid line numbers are rejected.

The native renderer inserts a replaced element once, relayouts when text changes, and forgets deleted nodes. The wasm host clamps guest indices, bounds-checks guest pointers, rejects tree cycles, derives the root at commit, and reports `OutOfFuel`.

The CLI always lets cargo decide what to recompile and caches only wasm-bindgen and `wasm-opt`, honours `build.client_package`, features, plugin env, and rustflags, restores missing outputs, and scaffolds projects that build. `doctor` exits non-zero when a required tool is missing. `leptoskit_axum` sends `Vary: Accept-Encoding`, limits the SPA fallback to page routes, and errors on an invalid bind address. `leptoskit_rpc` retries work in the browser. `leptoskit_config` validates package ids and code push settings.

The project has a logo, a documentation site, and a brand page.

changesets.summary: Publish the RPC: generated clients for any language
changesets.details: `#[leptoskit_rpc::api]` above `#[server]` publishes a server function: the route is pinned to a stable `/api/<name>`, the doc comment (including its `# Arguments` section) documents the function and each argument, and JSON Schemas generated through schemars describe every payload. `#[api(internal)]` leaves a function callable but takes it out of generated clients. Scaffold modes decide what regeneration may rewrite, and a new `[rpc]` section in leptoskit.toml names the clients, their directories, and exclusion globs. changesets.summary: Bound the cost of every code push request
changesets.details:
The code push server's dynamic `check`, `download`, and `delta` routes answered from a listing of the channel, so every request read, decompressed, and hash-checked every release on it. They now answer from `index.json` and at most two more files of the static layout, as the static routes always have: a request costs the same on a channel with a thousand releases as on one with two, and a flood of update checks can no longer be turned into disk and CPU work. A release whose files are on disk but which `index.json` does not name yet is not offered, which is the guarantee the static layout already made.

Storage failures in the code push routes and in `leptoskit_axum`'s SPA fallback are a `500` with a fixed message. Filesystem paths and file contents no longer reach the client.

changesets.summary: One dependency for the server
changesets.details:
A server package now depends on `leptoskit` alone. `leptos`, `leptos_router`, and `leptos_meta` are re-exported behind the `leptos` feature, and the new `csr`, `hydrate`, `ssr`, and `islands` features forward to them, so a package can write `hydrate = ["leptoskit/hydrate"]` instead of naming leptos; `server` implies `ssr`. `leptoskit build` turns islands on through `leptoskit/islands` when a package reaches leptos that way, and only requires a direct dependency on one of the two. A crate that uses leptos's macros still depends on `leptos` itself, because they expand to `::leptos::` paths.

`leptoskit_codepush` re-exports `ed25519_dalek` and `semver`, whose types sign and number every release.

changesets.summary: Add `leptoskit_l10n`: typed translations from ARB files
changesets.details:
Messages live in one ARB file per locale (`locales/en.arb`, `locales/pt-BR.arb`), with placeholders, ICU plurals (`{count, plural, =0 {none} one {# item} other {# items}}`), selects, and `@key` metadata that documents a message and types its placeholders. Turn translations on with an `[l10n]` table in `leptoskit.toml`, and the new `leptoskit l10n` command writes `src/l10n.rs`: a `Messages` trait with one method per message, typed by its placeholders and documented with its text; one implementation per locale, with untranslated messages falling back to the template; and the `L10n` handle an app reads them through. `dev`, `build`, and native builds regenerate the module before compiling, and `leptoskit l10n --check` fails CI when it is stale. Every problem in the files is reported with its file and line.

The runtime crate, `leptoskit_l10n`, carries `Locale` tags, Flutter-style locale negotiation, CLDR plural rules for every language, an `Accept-Language` parser for server rendering, `navigator.languages` for the browser behind its `web` feature, and the reactive `L10n` handle: a view that reads a message renders again when the locale changes. `leptoskit_l10n_codegen` is the generator the CLI uses. The `leptoskit` meta crate re-exports the runtime behind the `l10n` feature.

changesets.summary: `leptoskit dev` runs every platform
changesets.details:
`leptoskit dev` now runs every platform in `app.platforms` that this machine can run, and keeps them all current: the web app as before, plus each native app on this machine, in every booted iOS Simulator, and on every attached Android device or emulator. When no simulator or emulator is running, the newest iPhone simulator or the first installed emulator boots. Enabled platforms this machine can't run are skipped with the reason. `--platform`, repeatable, runs only the platforms named and fails when one can't run here. App logs stream into the same terminal, each line marked with its platform. `--device`, also repeatable, narrows iOS and Android to the simulators (by name or UDID) and adb serials named, booting a named simulator that is shut down. Devices that never finish booting or stop answering adb are skipped with the reason instead of stalling `dev`.

Each native app is built and installed once. After that, a change rebuilds only its WebAssembly interface, which `dev` serves from a loopback server (Android reaches it through `adb reverse`); the running app swaps it in without being reinstalled, keeping its window and its unchanged controls. A new interface that fails to start leaves the last working one on screen. Only debug builds accept an interface from `dev`: development interfaces are unsigned, so a release build refuses them.

Ctrl-C or `SIGTERM` stops `dev` cleanly, along with the app server and the desktop apps it opened.

Under that:

- `WasmHost::replace_guest` replaces a running guest while keeping the surface and the widgets it committed. The new guest's first commit is diffed against them.
- `NativeSurface::viewport` returns the viewport a surface lays out against.
- `leptoskit_axum::shutdown_signal`, also at `leptoskit::server::shutdown_signal`, resolves on Ctrl-C or `SIGTERM`, the signals `serve_listener` finishes its requests on.
- `leptoskit_codepush::dev` defines the development guest protocol, one long-polled `GET` per platform, with the `DevGuests` client and `follow_environment` for desktop runners behind the `http` feature. `leptoskit` exposes them through the new `codepush-http` feature.
- `leptoskit_bridge_ffi` adds `lk_dev_open`, `lk_dev_next`, `lk_dev_error`, and `lk_dev_destroy`. The generated iOS, macOS, and Android apps use them to follow `dev` without changes to their app-owned files.

Projects created before this release keep working. Their app-owned Linux and Windows runners open under `dev` but need a restart to show a change; to reload in place, copy the reload from a new project's `src/main.rs` and add `codepush-http` to the runner's `leptoskit` features.

`leptoskit native build ios` and `ios-simulator` remove `LD` and `LDPLUSPLUS` from Xcode's environment, so iOS builds work from a nix or devenv shell, which sets `LD=ld`.

changesets.summary: Benchmark leptoskit against React Native, Lynx, and Flutter
changesets.details:
The arena (`benchmarks/arena`) compares leptoskit with the latest releases of React Native, Lynx, and Flutter on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux, and the web. Each framework gets one self-driving app built from a shared contract.

The scenarios cover:

- **Cold open**: launch to the ready screen.
- **Big bang**: mount, update, and clear 1,000 cards.
- **Echo**: native-call round trips at five payload sizes, on the async and sync tiers.
- **Ticker wall, autoscroll, and busy hands**: frame scenarios.
- **Size tiers**: the same app at 1, 12, and 120 screens.

Frames are counted from screen recordings rather than from each framework's own counters. Every app shows a phase-coloured beacon, and the recording's deduplicated frames give presented frames per second and Apple's hitch-time ratio.

The tasks are:

- `benchmark:arena` runs every reachable target.
- `benchmark:arena:update` first moves every framework to its latest stable release, resolved from npm, Maven Central, CocoaPods, and Flutter's release feed.
- `benchmark:arena:docs` regenerates the comparison tables.

The new section in the Benchmarks chapter adds a table comparing the four frameworks' architectures: how updates and native calls cross to the screen, threading, 3D support, and over-the-air updates. An on-demand `arena` workflow measures Windows and Linux.

changesets.summary: Add `leptoskit_db_schema` for generated migrations
changesets.details: The first piece of leptoskit's built-in database layer. A database schema (tables, typed columns, keys, unique and partial indexes, foreign keys, checks, comments, and namespaces) is described once and compared with the snapshot committed beside the previous migration, producing a step-by-step plan and the SQL that applies it, for Postgres and SQLite. Renames come from explicit hints, or from a question when a column or table appears while a similar one disappears, so data is never dropped by a guess. Every step says what it risks for existing rows, and steps that delete data are called out. SQLite migrations rebuild tables whenever `ALTER TABLE` can't make a change, keeping every row and checking every foreign key. changesets.summary: Declare database tables as Rust structs

changesets.summary: Render native updates with a fraction of the work
changesets.details:
Native apps run their screens as WebAssembly in an interpreter, so the work a render does inside the guest dominates how fast an update reaches the screen. Three changes cut that work:

- An update sends the host only the elements whose properties changed. Unchanged elements reuse the bytes encoded by the previous render.
- Each distinct Tailwind class string is parsed once, rather than once per element on every render.
- Unset properties, a default layout style, and an empty class list are left out of what the guest sends the host. A typical element now encodes to a few dozen bytes instead of about a kilobyte. Every host and renderer already reads a missing property as unset, so this works in both directions with code push: old bundles keep working with new hosts, and new bundles with old hosts.

In the arena's big-bang scenario on macOS, creating 1,000 cards went from 726 ms to 517 ms, and updating every tenth card from 300 ms to 67 ms.

changesets.summary: Wait for the display with `leptoskit::guest::next_frame`
changesets.details:
Native apps can now animate from app code in step with the display. `leptoskit::guest::next_frame().await` resolves once per display frame on iOS and macOS (`CADisplayLink`) and Android (`Choreographer`). The host lets the app render inside that frame's callback, so a render that fits in a frame reaches the screen on the next vsync.

Before this, an app had to write its own frame plugin. Each frame then crossed several main-thread task hops and a paused display link, and that cost three to four frames per update.

The clock is a reserved plugin on the existing bridge, not a new WebAssembly import. A bundle that uses it still loads on apps built before it existed, where `next_frame` returns `Error::Unavailable`, so code push can deliver it safely. Hosts without a display link do the same: Windows, Linux, and HarmonyOS.

Hosts that embed `leptoskit_bridge_ffi` directly opt in with `lk_app_enable_frames`, then call `lk_app_frame` from their display link while `lk_app_frame_requested` is 1.

changesets.summary: Lay out only what a change can affect
changesets.details:
Native layout now stops at a relayout boundary, the way Flutter does. A boundary is an element whose parent sets both its width and its height without measuring its content, like a `flex-1` cell in a fixed-height row. When something inside a boundary changes, only that element's subtree is laid out again, not its siblings or ancestors.

A grid of cells whose labels change on every frame now costs the changed cells, not the whole grid. Two further changes make that possible and speed up every layout:

- A single-line container with a fixed cross size no longer measures the content of children it stretches, because the CSS algorithm never uses that measurement.
- Layout no longer copies each element's style on every pass.

Layouts are unchanged. A differential test compares incremental layout with a fresh layout across 2,000 random trees.

changesets.summary: Flatten layout-only views
changesets.details:
Containers that only arrange their children no longer get a native view in the generated iOS, Android, macOS, and HarmonyOS apps. That's a `View` with no background, border, rounded corners, opacity, clipping, hiding, accessibility label or role, or id. Its children join the nearest native ancestor at the same position on screen, so each flattened container saves creating, laying out, and compositing one view. React Native's Fabric does the same.

A container that later needs a view, because it gained a background for example, becomes one in place and takes its children back. Taps and accessibility are unchanged: events are dispatched on leptoskit's own tree, and a flattened container had no accessible role to begin with.

A differential test drives a surface through random screens and edits, and checks after every commit that each drawn element keeps its position, properties, and sibling order. It covers more than 8,000 flattened containers and 400 promotions.

changesets.summary: Render native screens with fewer interpreter instructions
changesets.details:
Native apps run their screens as WebAssembly in an interpreter, so every instruction a render executes costs real time. Counting them for the arena's ticker screen (920 elements, with 300 labels changing every frame) showed three avoidable costs, now gone:

- `.class(...)` built its combined class string with `format!`, which cost more than looking the parsed classes up. It now uses the string as given, or joins two strings directly.
- The parsed-class cache hashed every lookup with SipHash. It now uses a fast word-at-a-time hash, as rustc does for its own maps.
- The guest kept its tree in a `BTreeMap` of large nodes, so every render paid a tree lookup and shifted entries on each insert. It now uses a reserved hash map, plus a list of ids in build order, so the host still receives parents before children in a deterministic order.

`.children(...)` also reserves room for its children up front, rather than growing and moving its list.

A ticker frame went from 16.4 million interpreter instructions to 10.1 million, and a render with nothing changed from 13.6 million to 7.0 million. In the arena on macOS, updating every tenth of 1,000 cards went from about 51 ms to 32 ms, and the ticker from about 150 to about 170 updates in five seconds. Rendered output is unchanged.

changesets.summary: Build mobile screens several times faster
changesets.details:
Profiling the generated iOS and Android apps while they create, update and clear 1,000 cards found work that grew with the size of the screen, and work done for nothing. All of it is gone:

- **iOS inserts.** Reading `UIView.subviews` copies the whole child list, and each insert read it twice. Inserting 1,000 cards spent over 200 ms there; the renderer now counts children itself.
- **The interpreter.** Native apps ran their WebAssembly with a portable dispatch loop. They now use the interpreter's tail-call dispatch, which runs app code about two and a half times faster.
- **View flattening.** Finding a view's native position summed every earlier sibling, so it grew with each one. Appending now takes constant time: 17 ms to under 1 ms for 1,000 cards.
- **Text measurement.** Layout measured each label three or four times, under different heights it doesn't depend on. Each label is now measured once per width. iOS also reuses its fonts and text attributes instead of building them for every label.
- **Empty renders.** A native app pumps after every plugin reply and display frame, and asked for a render each time, encoding, decoding and applying an empty transaction. `lk_app_render_pending` now says when there is nothing to send, and the generated iOS and Android apps skip those renders. A plugin call with a small payload went from about 19 µs to 9 µs on both.
- **Comparing memory.** WebAssembly can copy memory in bulk but not compare it, so Rust compared byte by byte inside the interpreter. Guests now compare eight bytes at a time, so checking a 64 KiB reply takes 0.05 ms instead of 0.4.
- **A binary render transaction.** The generated iOS and Android apps read each render with `lk_app_render_binary`: fixed-width fields, read with a cursor, instead of JSON that Swift's `JSONDecoder` took 30 ms to decode for 1,000 cards and Android parsed into a tree of objects. It carries exactly what the JSON transaction does, which stays available through `lk_app_render`; properties the renderers apply to every view are typed fields, and any other property travels in its JSON form. A shared fixture holds the Rust encoder, the Swift decoder and the Kotlin decoder to the same bytes.
- **Native views.** Both renderers set a property only when it changes, reuse fonts and colors, and recycle the plain containers and labels a cleared screen leaves behind, as React Native does. Android no longer allocates a background drawable for every view, and keeps a view's layout parameters when its frame is unchanged.

In the arena on the iPhone simulator, creating 1,000 cards went from 583 ms to 150 ms, updating every tenth from 54 ms to 18 ms, and clearing them from 54 ms to 20 ms; a 64 KiB plugin round trip went from 1.8 ms to 0.09 ms. On the Android emulator, creating them went from 550 ms to 77 ms, updating from 100 ms to 18 ms, and clearing from 50 ms to 17 ms.

changesets.summary: Scroll from code, and report scrolls in generated apps

A list can now be moved by the app, not only by the person holding it: a "jump to today" button, a chat that follows its newest message, a feed that scrolls itself.

use leptoskit::native::ScrollOffset;

ScrollView().scroll_offset(ScrollOffset::new(0.0, 800.0).animated())

changesets.summary: Run iOS and Android screens off the main thread

The apps `leptoskit new` generates for iOS and Android now run your screens' code on a thread of its own. - **Plugin calls** to Swift and Kotlin handlers start in place, so a handler that answers at once replies without waiting for another turn of the main thread.

changesets.summary: Row-level security covers views and the audit log
changesets.details:
With `[db] policies = "rls"`, plain views on Postgres now read their tables as whoever reads them (`security_invoker`), so the tables' policies filter a view too, whoever owns it. Before, a view owned by a superuser, such as one created by a migration run as one, read every row. Materialized views are refreshed bypassing the policies, so they hold every row whoever refreshes them.

The audit log gets a policy of its own: raw SQL reads it only from a request holding an `AuditReader`, requests can add entries, and only `db.system(…)` can change or remove one. Before, the audit log had no policy, so raw SQL from any request could read it.

changesets.summary: Faster web renders and reconciles; rate limits that run
changesets.details:
A web re-render built every element's utility stylesheet twice — once only to hash it into a style scope — and hashed the result with SHA-256 on every rebuild, for every element, even when the document already carried the sheet. The scope now derives from the same content through the normalized class string, which determines the stylesheet, and the sheet itself is built only for a scope the document has not seen. Equal styles share one sheet exactly as before; only the scope names differ.

Reconciling a commit cloned every container's child list and deep-cloned every flattened node's props just to ask whether the node draws anything of its own, allocations on every frame's hot path. The child snapshot now lives in scratch space reused across commits, and the layout-only check compares fields in place — with the field list matched exhaustively, so a property added to `NativeProps` must be considered there to compile, and an unlisted one keeps its container a native view, the safe default. Production web builds also no longer format a devtools path for every node on every render when the devtools feature is off.

The server toolkit now serves with the peer address attached, so the auth layer's per-IP rate limits run in projects started from the scaffold: they read `ConnectInfo`, which plain `axum::serve` never fills in, and silently did nothing without it. Password reset also no longer runs Argon2 before the email code's rate limits have been paid for a guess. A channel index larger than its kind's bound is refused before it is parsed, a device remembers at most 64 rejected releases instead of every one forever, `leptoskit skill` refuses file names that would install outside its folder, a docs component link with a scheme a page cannot navigate to is a build error, and publishing to a plain-http S3 endpoint says what that exposes.

The wire error's constructors compile with the server's live module that calls them, so narrower builds — an app's server depending on `leptoskit_auth` alone — stay warning-clean too, and two stray debug prints are gone from the live client's tests.

changesets.summary: Add ARIA accessibility across every platform
changesets.details:
Every element now carries ARIA-shaped props — accessible names and descriptions (with id references), roles, states, range values, live regions, modal flags, set positions, orientation, tab order, and a passthrough for any other `aria-*` attribute — rendered as real attributes and semantic HTML elements on the web (headings, lists, landmarks, `<hr>` separators) and mapped onto each platform's accessibility API: VoiceOver traits on iOS, NSAccessibility roles and announcements on macOS, TalkBack class names and live regions on Android, MSAA roles with UIA control types and notifications on Windows, and GTK accessible properties, states, and relations.

Built-in components carry their semantics: Heading, Status, and Alert join the vocabulary; dividers are separators; lists, tiles, the app bar banner, and the scaffold main landmark announce their structure; activity indicators are named; and controls with a declared control role join the tab order and activate from Enter and Space. Validation rejects nameless text inputs and pressables, duplicate or dangling relationship ids, named presentation, and passthrough attributes that shadow typed builders.

The widget wire stays additive: `accessibility_label` keeps its key, unknown roles decode to none, and the resolver folds labelled-by and described-by references into concrete labels for native backends, numbers radio options within their group, and fills live-region announcement text. The widget tester gains `Finder::aria_role` and a semantics tree dump; the AppKit, browser, and widget suites cover the mapping, and the gallery demonstrates headings and a typing-indicator status region.

Focus scopes, traps, and custom accessibility actions remain pending; runtime services such as announcements outside live regions, screen-reader detection, and reduce-motion belong in a follow-up accessibility runtime plugin.

changesets.summary: One sign-in client for every platform
changesets.details:
`leptoskit::auth::client` now works the same in the browser and in native apps on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, and Linux: the same functions, the same arguments, and the same behaviour. A sign-in screen and a devices screen are written once, with no platform checks.

- **`configure(ClientConfig::new().origin(…).device_name(…))`** tells the client where the server is, once at startup, on every platform. On the web the origin defaults to the page's own.
- **`verify_code()`** takes `EmailCode { email, code }`. The client decides how the device keeps its session.
- **In the browser**, the session stays in the `HttpOnly` cookie, and the client keeps nothing scripts could read.
- **In a native app**, the client keeps the access token in memory and the refresh token in the secure store. It renews the access token when it runs out, one renewal at a time, and signs the app out when the session has ended elsewhere.
- **During server rendering**, `use_auth()` and `use_devices()` read the request's session directly.
- **`revoke_other_devices()` and `sign_out_everywhere_mutation()`** now return `()`.
- **New error codes:** `config` when the app isn't set up to reach the server, and `storage` when the secure store fails.

The client uses the `/auth` routes on every platform, and the facade's `web` and `guest` features choose how it reaches the server.

changesets.summary: Two-step sign-in, and sign-in in native guests
changesets.details:
An emailed code proves only that someone can read the inbox. Accounts can now turn on an authenticator app, so whoever gets into a person's email still can't get into their account, and sensitive actions can ask for a fresh code. It works the same in the browser and in native apps.

- **Authenticator apps (TOTP):** `enroll_totp()` and `confirm_totp()` turn one on with a code from it, so a mistyped secret never locks anyone out. Once it's on, `verify_code()` answers `SignInStep::SecondFactor`, and `complete_sign_in()` finishes with the app's code. Codes work once, and the secret is encrypted in the database with AES-256-GCM-SIV under `AUTH_ENCRYPTION_KEYS`.
- **Recovery codes:** ten, shown once when the authenticator is turned on, each signing in once if the phone is lost. Using one signs out every other device and emails the account. `regenerate_recovery_codes()` replaces them.
- **Step-up:** `auth::require_step_up(auth::STEP_UP_WINDOW)` in a server function asks for a code from the last ten minutes; the client answers `step_up_required` with `step_up()` and tries again. Stepping up replaces the session's token.
- **Screens:** `leptoskit generate auth` and `leptoskit new --auth` write a two-step verification screen and a `/security` route, and the sign-in screen asks for the second step when an account has one.
- **Native guests:** a native app built with `--auth` now loads and runs its sign-in screens. Browser-only timers no longer reach native builds, the native runtime tells guests the time through a new optional `leptoskit_clock` export, wasm-bindgen glue that only a browser could call links to a trap that names it instead of stopping the app from loading, and the `http` and `secure-store` plugins are granted and added to the iOS, Android, and macOS hosts. The Linux, Windows, and terminal runners can't host plugins yet: they now build without them, with a warning, instead of refusing to build.

changesets.summary: Native sign-in tokens and a list of signed-in devices
changesets.details:
Native apps have no cookies, so a single long-lived token was all they had. Now they get two:

- **An access token** for each request, which works for 15 minutes (`[auth] access_minutes`, up to 60).
- **A refresh token** for the platform's secure store. It trades for a new pair at `POST /auth/refresh` and works once. If a used one turns up again after a 30-second grace, the session ends: someone else has a copy.

Browsers keep their `HttpOnly` cookie, which scripts can't read. Every token is random rather than signed, and checked on every request, so ending a session takes effect at once.

People can also see where they're signed in and end any of it:

- **`GET /auth/sessions`** lists each device, marking the current one.
- **`POST /auth/sessions/revoke-all`** and **`auth.sign_out_everywhere(account)`** end every session, the current one included.
- **The headless client** adds `use_devices()`, `revoke_device()`, `revoke_other_devices()` and `sign_out_everywhere_mutation()`.
- **Device names:** a native app can name its device, such as "Ada's iPhone", when it signs in.

`SignedInResponse.token` is now `tokens`.

changesets.summary: Passkeys and provider sign-in in native apps
changesets.details:
Native apps now sign in with passkeys and with Google, Apple, Microsoft, GitHub, and any OpenID Connect provider, through the same `leptoskit::auth::client` functions as the web. App code doesn't change.

- **Two new plugins.** `passkeys` uses the system's own sheet: `ASAuthorization` on iOS and macOS, Credential Manager on Android, and Sign in with Apple's own sheet for Apple on Apple devices. `web-auth` signs in with other providers in the system browser, never a web view in the app: `ASWebAuthenticationSession` on iOS and macOS, Auth Tab on Android (Chrome 137 or later), and a loopback address in the default browser for Windows and Linux hosts that register it.
- **The flow.** The provider sends the browser back to your site's `/auth/callback/…`, as for the web, so providers need no new setup. Your site sends the browser on to the app with the provider's answer, and the app finishes at `POST /auth/oauth/finish` with a binding only it holds, so an intercepted answer or a link someone else started signs no one in. `sign_in_with_provider()` resolves once the browser is back, and `provider_outcome()` says how it ended.
- **Your site vouches for its apps.** Set `apple_team_id` and `android_certificates` in `[native]`, and merge `leptoskit::server::app_associations` (or the generated `sign_in::associations()`) into your router: it serves `/.well-known/apple-app-site-association` and `/.well-known/assetlinks.json` from `[native]`. The server then accepts the Android app's passkeys, and Sign in with Apple ID tokens for your bundle ID.
- **Scaffold.** `leptoskit new --auth` and `leptoskit generate auth` grant `passkeys` and `web-auth` alongside `http` and `secure-store`, and the generated server serves the association files.

Native apps don't offer passkeys in a text field's suggestions; the generated Xcode projects don't add the associated-domain or Sign in with Apple entitlements yet; Android has no fallback for browsers without Auth Tab; and Windows and Linux have no native passkeys.

changesets.summary: Passkeys, required two-step, and account lockout
changesets.details:
`leptoskit::auth` signs people in with passkeys on the web, and can require two-step verification.

- **Passkeys** (the `auth-passkeys` feature on your server, plus `[auth] origin`): `add_passkey()`, `passkey_sign_in()` from a button or from the email field's suggestions (`PasskeyMode::Autofill`, with the field's new `.autocomplete("username webauthn")`), `complete_sign_in_with_passkey()` as the second step, `step_up_with_passkey()`, and `use_passkeys()`, `rename_passkey()`, and `remove_passkey()`. A passkey that verifies its user signs in at `aal2` on its own. The functions exist on every platform; native apps answer `unsupported` until their passkey plugin arrives.
- **Required two-step verification:** `[auth] mfa = "required"`, or `required_for = ["Admin"]` with `AuthBuilder::roles::<User>()`. Until someone sets up a factor, their session can only do that; everything else answers `mfa_required`.
- **Account lockout:** after 20 wrong second factors in a day, sign-in is locked for an hour and the owner is emailed. `Auth::unlock` lifts it, and `Auth::reset_mfa` removes an account's authenticator, recovery codes, and passkeys for someone locked out of their own.
- **QR codes:** `client::qr_code(&setup.uri)` draws the authenticator setup link as a `Vector` path or SVG, made on the device.
- **`leptoskit auth rotate-keys`** re-encrypts stored secrets under the newest key, and **`leptoskit auth doctor`** checks `[auth]` without printing secrets; `--release` fails on plain `http` origins and the development mailbox.

changesets.summary: Solana wallets, and merging accounts with their data
changesets.details:
`leptoskit::auth` links Solana wallets to accounts (the `auth-solana` feature on your server, plus `[auth] origin`), and merges two accounts with the other account's data.

- **Link a wallet** with `link_wallet()`: the person's wallet signs a Sign-In With Solana message bound to your site, with a single-use nonce that expires in five minutes, and the server checks it byte for byte and as ed25519. In the browser, any wallet that supports the Wallet Standard works; `use_wallet_apps()` lists them.
- **Wallets are private, and don't sign in, until the person says so.** `update_wallet()` shows one on their profile (`auth.public_wallets(account)`) or lets it sign in, with `[auth.solana] sign_in = true` on the server. `wallet_sign_in()` is one factor, so two-step verification still applies. `unlink_wallet()` removes one.
- **Fresh proofs:** `auth.require_wallet_proof(&me, &address, window)` answers `proof_required` until the wallet signs again with `prove_wallet()`, for payouts and other actions tied to the address.
- **Rules can name a wallet's owner:** `vault.treasury.in_list(cx.wallets())`.
- **New scalars:** `leptoskit::db::Pubkey` and `Signature`, base58 text that must decode to exactly 32 or 64 bytes. Scalars can run their own check with `#[db(validate_with = …)]`.
- **Merge with the data:** `MergeMode::BringData` moves the other account's rows into this one, each table as its `#[db::table(on_account_merge = …)]` strategy says: `reassign` (the default), `reassign_skip_conflicts`, `keep_newest`, `keep_survivor`, or `custom` with your `auth::OnMerge`. The merge offer previews its data (`MergeOffer::data`), and a failure changes nothing. `leptoskit db check` fails until every table that could collide declares a strategy.
- `lk generate auth` adds wallets and the merge preview to the security screen, and wallet buttons to the sign-in screen.
- The functions exist on every platform. Native apps manage linked wallets, and answer `unsupported` for asking a wallet to sign until a native wallet adapter exists.

changesets.summary: Browser extensions
changesets.details:
An app can now be a browser extension for Chromium browsers, Firefox, and Safari, built from the same routes as its website and native apps. Add `extension` to `app.platforms`, describe the surfaces in `[extension]`, and run `leptoskit build --platform extension`.

- **Content scripts** run the app in a frame of the extension's own page, inside a closed shadow root, because most large sites forbid compiling WebAssembly in their pages. `leptoskit::extension::page` reads the page's details and selection, places the frame, and highlights quotes. changesets.summary: Show buttons as pressed while they are held
changesets.details:
A styled button showed no change while you pressed it, on the web and on every native platform. `Button` and `Pressable` now accept `active:` utilities, such as `active:bg-indigo-700 active:opacity-80`, and apply them while the control is held down: through CSS `:active` on the web, and through each platform's own pressed state on macOS, iOS, Android, Linux, and Windows. The web adapter's rendered root now listens passively for touches, because iOS Safari applies `:active` to a touched element only where the page listens for them. Only the held control is restyled, in place, keeping its accessible name and role. `active:` on any other element is a `ClassError`, since native platforms report presses only for controls.

Controls without `active:` utilities now dim to 70 percent of their opacity while held: every `Pressable`, and every `Button` with its own background, border, or corner radius. Buttons that keep their native chrome keep the platform's own highlight instead. The Windows backend no longer darkens held pressables, or buttons with their own background, border, or corners, on top of that, and Android buttons in non-scrolling containers show their pressed state on touch down rather than after the tap delay.

Backends report holds as the new `NativeEvent::PressIn` and `NativeEvent::PressOut`. `WasmHost::dispatch` handles them on the host without entering the guest, and other hosts pass them to the new `NativeSurface::press_in` and `NativeSurface::press_out`. `StyleContext::active` resolves a tree with its controls pressed, `lk_app_event` accepts kinds 8 and 9 for the generated apps' renderers, and `WidgetTester::hold` and `release` let widget tests check pressed styles. changesets.summary: Make code push deltas pay off and harden the update paths
changesets.details:
Deltas used to be computed between gzip streams, which differ in every byte after the first change, and stored inserted bytes as a pretty-printed JSON array, so a delta was usually larger than the full download. Containers now compress each file in chunks of about 64 KiB that come out the same whenever their input does, so a delta carries only the chunks an update changed; inserted bytes travel as base64 in compact JSON; and `release` keeps a delta only when it is at most three quarters of the full container. Containers stay ordinary gzip, so older clients read them unchanged; a delta in the new encoding fails to parse on an older client, which falls back to the full download. Chunked compression makes a container up to a few percent larger than plain gzip.

A release that failed activation on a device is no longer downloaded again on every check: while the channel still names it, `InstalledBundles::sync` reads only `index.json` and reports the working release as current, instead of downloading up to 32 MiB and failing.

`CodePushClient::with_max_container_bytes` now bounds full downloads and delta bodies as well as delta output, and `CodePushClient::sync` replaces its staging directory whole, so files of the previous release no longer survive an update and a failed sync leaves the previous staging intact.

The release store assembles each release directory, container, signature, and delta, under a temporary name and renames it into place, so a crash can no longer leave an unsigned release that blocks re-releasing that version. `pull` checks the bucket's container against the signed manifest before decompressing anything, and containers with bytes after their last file, or after a file's gzip stream, are rejected. The code push routes log the cause of every `500` through `tracing`, while the client still sees only a fixed message.

changesets.summary: Trial and roll back installed native bundles
changesets.details:
`leptoskit_codepush::installed::InstalledBundles` owns the release a native shell runs. `sync_with` downloads and verifies an update and stores the signed container without running it. It also refuses bundles whose `runtime.json` names a different native ABI or shell contract, or a plugin the shell lacks. `launch` marks a downloaded release as a trial before returning its Wasm. `confirm` promotes it once the host has rendered it, and `reject` drops it and keeps the last working release. A trial left unconfirmed by process death is rejected on the next open. Confirmed releases load offline and have their signatures checked again on every launch. A newer store baseline supersedes older downloads.

The `http` feature adds a blocking `HttpTransport` for a serialized background worker. It requires HTTPS unless plaintext is explicitly allowed, follows no redirects, caps responses at 32 MiB, and gives each request 30 seconds. `CodePushClient::download_verified` authenticates an update without staging it or advancing the running release, and `bundle_directory_as` packs a store baseline with an explicit identity.

changesets.summary: Geospatial columns on PostGIS and SQLite
changesets.details:
The `db-geo` feature adds `leptoskit::db::geo`: `Geography<Point>` for places on the globe, measured in metres, and `Geo<Polygon, Srid<27700>>` for planar shapes in any coordinate system, where mixing systems fails to compile. Postgres uses PostGIS, created by the first migration that needs it, with GiST indexes, and adds `buffer`, `simplify`, `transform`, and `union`. SQLite uses a built-in layer with nothing to install: GeoPackage-encoded columns checked by the database, an R*Tree per index kept current by triggers, and functions registered on every connection, measuring the globe with the same geodesic algorithm as PostGIS. `[db.geo] geopackage = true` makes a SQLite file open as layers in QGIS and GDAL.

changesets.summary: Hooks, an audit log, and views in the database
changesets.details:
`hooks(before_write, after_insert, after_update, after_delete)` on `#[db::table]` runs your own `BeforeWrite`, `AfterInsert`, `AfterUpdate`, and `AfterDelete` code inside every single-row write's transaction, so a failing hook rolls the write back. `before_write` sees whether it's an insert and the row as stored before an update. Bulk updates and deletes, which never load rows, fail with `DbError::HooksSkipped` on a table whose hooks they'd skip, unless told `.allow_skipping_hooks()`.

`#[db(created_by)]` and `#[db(updated_by)]` record who inserted and last wrote a row, from the request's `Actor`, which sign-in adds for every signed-in request. A required one refuses a write with nobody acting. `#[db(slug(from = title), unique)]` fills in a unique URL slug on insert, such as `hello-world-2`.

`#[db::table(audit)]` records every insert, update, and delete in `_leptoskit_audit`, in the same transaction: who made it, the reason a `db.system("…")` bypass gave, and the row before and after, never its `secret` columns. A request reads no entry unless its context holds an `AuditReader`.

`#[db::view(name = "author_stats", sql = "SELECT …")]` declares a view that the migrations create and that's read like a table under its own `select` policies; `materialized` keeps its rows until `AuthorStats::refresh(&db)`, on Postgres and SQLite alike.

changesets.summary: Links, shapes, projections, and generated columns
changesets.details:
`#[db::link(name = "post_tags", from = Post as tags, to = Tag as posts)]` declares a table that links two others many to many, on a struct of the link's own columns. The macro adds the two ends as the table's key, deleted with either end, and generates `post.tags()` and `tag.posts()`: `add(&db, tag.id, PostTagProperties { position: 0 })`, `remove`, `all` (each tag with its link), `ids`, `count`, and `contains`, with `filter`, `filter_link`, `order_by`, `limit`, and `offset`. A link is only there when the request may see both its ends, and link tables take policies like any table. `exclusive` lets each row be linked from one row only, and a table can link to itself with `from_column` and `to_column`.

`#[derive(db::Shape)]` fetches a row and the rows linked to it in one statement: `#[db(count(posts))]` counts linked rows, and `#[db(via = posts, order_by = |post| post.created_at.desc(), limit = 3)]` nests them as another shape, through link columns, backlinks, and `#[db::link]` tables, on Postgres and SQLite alike. `User::query().filter(…).shape::<ProfileCard>().one(&db)` runs it. Every nested table's policies and soft deletes apply, and a `public` shape fails to compile if it reads a private column or nests a shape that isn't public.

`projection(SelfUser)` on a table, with `#[db(private, in(SelfUser))]` on a column, generates a second client type that shows that private column, such as the signed-in user's own email.

`#[db(generated = "lower(handle)", unique)]` declares a column the database computes from the row's other columns and stores, so it can be indexed and unique; `generated(postgres = "…", sqlite = "…")` gives each database its own expression. Inserts, upserts, and saves never write it and return the computed value, and setting one in a bulk update fails. Migrations add and drop them on both databases.

changesets.summary: Live changes, push mode, and branch databases
changesets.details:
`#[db::table(live)]` publishes every committed write: `db.changes().await?` gives a request a feed of `Invalidation`s naming the tables and keys that changed, filtered by its `select` policy before and after each change, so nobody learns of rows they can't see. Postgres carries changes between servers with `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY`; SQLite keeps them in the process. With `leptoskit_query`'s `db` feature, `table_tag`, `row_tag`, and `QueryClient::apply_invalidation` refetch exactly the queries a change touches.

`[db] watch = "push"` makes `leptoskit dev` apply table changes to the development database without writing migrations; `leptoskit db migration create` then writes one migration for all of them and the database takes it over, rows intact. Pushes that delete data need `leptoskit db push --allow-destructive`, and a database with pushes refuses migrations it hasn't had.

On the development Postgres each git branch gets its own database, copied from the main branch's the first time; `leptoskit dev` follows `git switch`, and `leptoskit db branch list` and `prune --yes` clean up after finished branches. `branch_databases = false` turns it off.

changesets.summary: Full-text search and row-level security
changesets.details:
Mark text columns with `#[db(search)]`, or `#[db(search(weight = A))]` to make a match there count more, and `Article::query().search("passkeys rust")` returns the matching rows best first. The query reads like a search box (`"phrases"`, `-excluded`, `OR`, `prefix*`), and nothing typed into it is ever SQL syntax. `hits()` returns each row's rank and, with `highlight(…)` and `excerpt(…, words)`, its matching words marked as plain-text segments rather than HTML. The table's `select` policy, soft deletes, filters, and paging apply as to any query. Postgres keeps a generated `tsvector` column with a GIN index; SQLite keeps an FTS5 table and a key map that triggers update on every write, raw SQL included. `search(language = "english")` stems words; the default, `simple`, matches them as written.

On Postgres, `[db] policies = "rls"` also enforces access policies as row-level security, so raw SQL is filtered too. Rules read the request through settings, `cx.setting::<Viewer>()`, from types that implement `Setting` and are registered with `register_setting!`; migrations create a policy per command, and `Db::with_row_security()` tells Postgres who each transaction acts for. Results are the same with it on and off. `leptoskit_auth`'s tables read the signed-in account as a setting.

changesets.summary: Polymorphic tables and the database studio

A link can now point at one of several tables. changesets.summary: Read-only connections, read sets, in-memory conditions
changesets.details:
`leptoskit_db` and `leptoskit_rpc` gain what live queries build on:

- **`db::Read`.** Every read (queries, counts, `get`, `find`, link accessors, shapes, searches, `nearest`, polymorphic reads, and views) takes `&impl db::Read`, and writes still take `&impl db::Connection`, which now extends it. `Db` and `Tx` are both, so code passing them keeps compiling. `Db::dialect` and `Tx::dialect` are now inherent, so code that imported `Connection` only to call `dialect()` can drop the import; code that called the hidden `fetch` on a `Db` imports `db::Read` instead.
- **`db::Tracked`.** A read-only connection that records each read: the table, the filter combined with the access policy and soft deletes, the order, limit and offset, the kind of read, and the keys of the rows returned. Policy subqueries, link tables, each level of a shape, and searches get their own entries.
- **Raw SQL and views declare what they read.** `Statement::new(sql, args).reads::<Post>().fetch(&db)` and `#[db::view(reads(Post))]`; a tracked read that doesn't say fails with `DbError::UndeclaredRead`.
- **`Expr::eval`.** A condition can be checked against one row's values without the database, in SQL's three-valued logic. It answers "false" only when both Postgres and SQLite would certainly not match, and "unknown" for anything dialect- or collation-sensitive, or that reads other rows.
- **`HasId` on client types.** `Public…` types, projections, and public shapes that select their table's `id` implement `HasId<Table>`. `HasId` now takes the table as a parameter (`HasId<T = Self>`) and no longer requires `Table`.
- **Queries can't write.** `QueryCx::db()` is a `Tracked<Db>`, so a write in an `#[rpc::query]` body fails to compile. `QueryCx::reads()` returns its read set, and `rpc::server::ReadSink`, passed in `Invocation::reads`, collects it from a query run by name.

changesets.summary: Vector columns on pgvector and SQLite
changesets.details:
The `db-vector` feature adds `leptoskit::db::vector`: `Vector<1536>` for embeddings, `HalfVector<N>` at half the size, `BitVector<N>` for binary quantisation, and `SparseVector<N>` for mostly-zero vectors on Postgres. The number of dimensions is part of the type, so a 768-dimension embedding can't be stored in, or searched against, a 1536-dimension column. Vectors travel as JSON (floats as arrays of numbers, bits as a string of `0` and `1`), and vector columns are private unless they say `#[db(public)]`.

`#[db(vector(distance = cosine, index = hnsw))]` declares how a column is measured: `l2`, `cosine`, `inner_product`, `l1`, `hamming`, or `jaccard`. `query().nearest(|a| a.embedding, &query_embedding).with_distance().limit(10)` returns the nearest rows first, with the table's filters, policies, and soft deletes applied. Postgres uses pgvector, created by the first migration that needs it, with HNSW or IVFFlat indexes for the column's distance, scanned until enough rows match the filters; `.exact()` skips them. SQLite needs nothing installed: sqlite-vec is compiled into the build, each indexed column gets a `vec0` table kept current by triggers, and every search is exact.

`query().hybrid(|h| h.text("passkeys in rust").vector(|a| a.embedding, &query_embedding))` ranks a searchable table by full-text relevance and vector similarity together, fused by reciprocal rank fusion.

A vector made from text columns, `source(title, body)`, records a fingerprint of them whenever it's written, so a write that changes only the text leaves it stale. `Article::stale_embeddings()` lists the rows to embed again, and `embed_stale(|a| a.embedding, &model, &db)` makes and stores their vectors with any model through the `Embedder` trait; none is wired in. `leptoskit db check` warns about vector columns clients can see, and, given a SQLite database, about tables past `[db.vector] exact_search_rows` rows.

changesets.details:
A server-rendered app needed hand-written container files and its own shutdown logic before it could run anywhere but your machine. Now:

- **`leptoskit generate deploy --target <docker|compose|fly>`** writes a multi-stage `Dockerfile` (a `leptoskit build --release`, then an unprivileged, read-only runtime with the `LEPTOS_*` environment and a health check) and a `.dockerignore`, plus `compose.yaml` with Postgres or a SQLite volume, or `fly.toml` with readiness checks, a kill timeout past the grace period, and machines that stay up for long-lived connections. changesets.summary: Native apps report to DevTools under `leptoskit dev`
changesets.details:

The iOS Simulator and Android emulator apps run the same code. Selecting a node highlights it, and picking takes the next tap on a control instead of passing it to the app. When `leptoskit dev` reloads the guest, the app keeps its session and sends the new tree once it renders.

- **Only in development.** `leptoskit dev` builds the debug host with `leptoskit_bridge_ffi`'s new `devtools` feature and the guest with the app's `devtools` feature, and tells the app where the hub is: `LEPTOSKIT_DEVTOOLS` on macOS, `SIMCTL_CHILD_LEPTOSKIT_DEVTOOLS` in the iOS Simulator, and the `leptoskit.devtools` intent extra on Android, whose device reaches the hub through `adb reverse`. `leptoskit build` never does, and a release build refuses to report even with the feature.

changesets.details:
A browser app under `leptoskit dev` now hands the DevTools what only it knows, through hooks in `leptoskit::devtools` that do nothing in any other build:

- **`track_router(&router)`** reports the current route as its href the moment the app navigates, and the route panel's **Navigate** parses an href and navigates the app, as a link would.
- **`expose("cart.count", signal)`** shows a signal as JSON with its Rust type, and the state panel edits it. Only state named this way appears.

changesets.details:
`leptoskit::idp` now covers the ways in beyond a browser's code flow, and the pieces apps need around it.

- **The device flow** (RFC 8628) for command-line tools and TVs: the device shows a code, the person enters it on your device page and approves. CLIs generated with `leptoskit rpc generate --target cli` get `login` and `logout` built on it when any function needs a scope, and keep their tokens in a file only you can read.
- **Apps acting as themselves** with `client_credentials`: access tokens with your API's own scopes and no person, which reach `#[api(scope = …)]` functions signed out.
- **Pushed authorization requests** (RFC 9126) at `/oauth/par`, form `POST`s to `/oauth/authorize` and `/oauth/end_session`, and the `claims` parameter for ID-token claims.
- **`private_key_jwt`** client authentication with ES256 or RS256 keys, and **RS256 ID tokens** for apps registered for them, from an RSA key in the environment.
- **A developer portal**, off by default: signed-in people register, change, rotate, and delete apps of their own through `/oauth/apps`.

- **The audit trail** records connecting and disconnecting apps, reused codes and refresh tokens, and portal changes in `auth.events`, naming the app. Other crates record their own events with `Auth::record`.
- **`[auth.idp]` in `leptoskit.toml`** configures pages, lifetimes, the RSA key, and the portal; `Idp::from_config` reads it.
- **`leptoskit auth idp client add`** takes `--grant code|device|machine`, `--jwks`, and `--rs256`, and `client rotate-secret` replaces a secret.

changesets.summary: Bind tokens to apps' keys, and let apps register
changesets.details:
`leptoskit::idp` gains two opt-in features, both off by default.

- **DPoP (RFC 9449):** with `dpop = true` in `[auth.idp]`, an app that sends a `DPoP` proof gets tokens bound to its key: the access token works at your API and `userinfo` only as `Authorization: DPoP` with a fresh proof from that key, and a public app's refresh token only with one too. A stolen token is useless without the key. `leptoskit auth idp client add --dpop` requires it of an app. Introspection reports the key as `cnf`, and discovery lists the proof algorithms.
- **Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591 and 7592):** with `dynamic_registration = true`, apps register themselves at `POST /oauth/register`, then read, change, and delete their registration with the token it returns. `registration_token_env` names an initial access token apps must send; without one, registration is open and limited to 10 apps an hour from one address. Self-registered apps are never first-party, can't introspect other apps' tokens, and are marked in `client list`.

changesets.summary: Let other apps sign in with yours
changesets.details:
`leptoskit::idp` turns your app into an OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect provider, so other websites, native apps, and command-line tools can offer "Sign in with" your app and call your API for the people who allow it.

- **The `idp` schema pack** keeps registered apps, consent grants, codes, refresh-token families, and the public halves of signing keys in your own database, next to the `auth` pack.
- **Standard endpoints:** discovery, JWKS, the authorization code flow with PKCE (`S256` only, exact redirect addresses), the token endpoint, `userinfo`, revocation, introspection, and RP-initiated logout.
- **Tokens:** 10-minute ES256 access tokens (RFC 9068), ID tokens, and refresh tokens that work once; using one twice ends every token from that sign-in. Each app sees its own `sub` for a person.
- **Your consent page:** `/oauth/authorize` sends people to a page you design, which reads the request and posts the answer as JSON. People see and disconnect apps through `/oauth/grants`.
- **Typed scopes:** declare them with `leptoskit::rpc::scopes!`, and require them with `#[api(scope = Scope::NotesRead)]`. A partner's token reaches only those functions, which run as the person who allowed it, so access policies apply unchanged. The OpenAPI document lists each function's scopes.

changesets.summary: Add document import, orientation and sensor capabilities
changesets.details:
Add independent `document_picker`, `screen_orientation`, `light_sensor` and `pedometer` crates with selected-plugin native registration and typed binary guest contracts.

Document picker imports one ordinary file through iOS, macOS, Android or a browser, with bounded off-thread native reads, balanced resource access and shared Rust reply storage. Windows/Linux hosts can use an explicit parent-window API. Directory selection, export, multiple files and persistent grants remain separate work.

Screen orientation reports the presented interface and holds a cancellable policy lease for the owning iOS scene, Android Activity or browser document. Cancellation and lifecycle cleanup release the request; a pending lease does not prove that the operating system rotated the interface. Native desktop locking is unavailable.

changesets.summary: Harden translations: names, variants, scripts, quoting
changesets.details:
`leptoskit l10n` now rejects, with the file and line, ARB files that used to generate a module that misbehaved or did not compile: a key that would become one of the `L10n` handle's own methods (`locale`, `set_locale`, `messages`, `clone`, `into`, and the rest), which `l10n.locale()` would call instead of the message; a key or placeholder named `gen`, reserved from Rust 2024; an `=N` form larger than its placeholder's type holds; and quoted text that reads as a placeholder, such as `'{name}'`, which a Flutter project without `use-escaping` means as the placeholder. A key that is not an identifier says why instead of calling it a keyword, and problems are listed by file and then by line. Outside a plural, `'#'` now stays as written, as in ICU.

Locales with variants, such as `ca-ES-valencia` next to `ca-ES`, each get their own messages, and a placeholder can no longer shadow a locale's plural rules. Forms with the same text share one `match` arm or `if` branch, a select or plural with only `other` is its text, and a placeholder a translation leaves unread is named `_name`, so the generated module passes clippy's pedantic lints. Message text holding backticks shows as code in the generated documentation. `leptoskit l10n --check` also stays green after rustfmt rewraps the module's documentation or splits its long strings.

Locale negotiation fills in the script CLDR expects for languages written in more than one, so `zh-TW` picks `zh-Hant` over `zh-Hans`, and the docs list where it chooses differently from Flutter. `accept_language` leaves out entries whose quality value RFC 9110 does not allow (`q=NaN`, `q=5`), and `browser_locales` is exported with or without the `web` feature, returning an empty list wherever there is no browser to ask.

changesets.summary: Capture live changes with triggers and commit versions
changesets.details:
Live tables now record their writes in the database itself, so every write reaches subscribers, whoever makes it, and nothing is lost when a connection drops.

- **Every writer counts.** Marking a table `live` gives it capture triggers in its next migration, which record each insert, update, and delete in the `live` pack's change log (`live.changes` and `live.commits`) in the writing transaction. Raw SQL, `psql`, other services, and the database's own `on_delete` cascades are captured like the app's own writes.
- **One version line.** Each commit that wrote a live table takes the next version: on Postgres at commit, under a transaction-scoped advisory lock, so versions become visible in order; on SQLite just before the pool commits. Rolled-back transactions take none.
- **Feeds read the log.** `db.changes()` works as before, and a feed now catches up from the log after a lagging subscriber or a lost `LISTEN` connection instead of returning `Invalidation::Everything`. `Feed::next_versioned()` returns each invalidation's version, and `db.changes_since(version)` resumes after it. `Everything` remains for a log pruned past the feed, or a table this build doesn't know.
- **Smaller columns, shorter logs.** `#[db(live = skip)]` keeps a column out of the log, as `secret` columns always are, and `Table::LIVE_COLUMNS` lists what is copied. `db.prune_changes(retention)` deletes old entries.
- **For servers.** `db.change_log(version)`, on a `system` handle, reads every commit with its rows' keys and images, for a hub that decides itself who may see what. `Tx::set_origin` records what made a commit, and RPC mutations record their own names.
- **Lighter writes.** Live tables no longer take the audit log's write path, and a transaction no longer buffers changes to publish. Audited tables behave as before.
- **`leptoskit db check --live`** checks a database's capture triggers, functions, and sequences against the schema. `leptoskit_db_schema` models sequences, functions, and triggers, including deferred constraint triggers, and diffs and renders them on both databases.

changesets.summary: Capture live changes by logical replication
changesets.details:
An app that commits thousands of transactions a second to live tables can now record their changes from Postgres's write-ahead log instead of with triggers. Set `[db] live_capture = "replication"`: the next migration drops the capture triggers and publishes the live tables, and `Db::capture_changes()` reads each committed transaction from a logical replication slot (`pgoutput`) into the same change log, with versions in commit order and each commit's write-ahead log position. Writers pay nothing extra, and feeds, invalidations, `Db::change_log`, and clients are unchanged. One server captures at a time, chosen by an advisory lock, and another takes over when it stops; the slot moves only after the log has the rows. `Db::live_stats()` reports how far capture lags (`live_capture_lag`), `Db::live_caught_up()` waits until the log has every commit made so far, and `leptoskit db check --live` warns when nothing is capturing. It needs `wal_level = logical` and a role with `REPLICATION`.

On Postgres the change log is now partitioned, commits by version and changes by their order, and the next migration rebuilds an existing log into partitions. Pruning keeps its marker commit and drops whole partitions rather than deleting rows. `Db::live_maintenance(retention, interval)` makes partitions ahead and prunes on a schedule, taking turns across servers, and `rpc::server::Jobs` starts it, and replication capture, with the workers: `[db] live_retention_minutes` (15 by default) says how much of the log to keep, and `Jobs::from_configs` reads it.

changesets.summary: Scale live servers: a relay, roles, read replicas
changesets.details:
Live queries and channels now scale past one database reader per server.

- **The live relay.** `rpc::server::Relay` (the `relay` feature, `rpc-relay` on the facade) connects to NATS JetStream. `relay.publish(&db)` publishes the change log from one server at a time, with a lease that another server takes over within five seconds, and `Live::relay(&relay)` makes a server take commits from the stream instead of reading the database. Commits arrive in order and once each, gaps are read from the database, and a server reads the database itself while no one publishes. Channel signals and presence cross between servers. `[rpc.live] relay_url_env` names the URL. `Live::start()` starts a server before its first connection, and `LiveStats` gains `relay_fills`.
- **Roles.** `rpc::server::Roles` reads `--role` or `LEPTOSKIT_ROLE` (`web`, `live`, `worker`, `capture`, any combination, every one by default). The scaffold's database servers serve their pages only with `web`. `leptoskit generate deploy --target kubernetes --split-roles` writes one Deployment per role on Postgres, and the Kubernetes manifests' `PodDisruptionBudget` kind is valid YAML again.
- **Read replicas.** `Db::with_replica(url)` and `[db] replica_url_envs` add Postgres standbys. A live query re-runs on one only once it has replayed past the commits that caused the re-run, and on the primary otherwise, so a screen never shows an older state; `LiveStats` gains `replica_reruns`. Other reads stay on the primary unless the app asks with `db.on_replica()`, whose `SELECT`s go to a replica while writes stay on the primary. Every change log `Commit` now carries `lsn`, the position a replica must reach to show it, and commits serialize.
- **`leptoskit_db`.** `Db::change_log_after(v)` reads one page of the change log without listening.

changesets.summary: Fix query lifecycle, cancellation, and cache identity
changesets.details:
Queries now leave the cache when they should and never take stale data:

- `use_queries` keeps every handle alive as its key list grows, rebinds when its queries are removed, and releases its observers on unmount, so those queries stop counting as active and are garbage collected. An observer that is dropped always unregisters from its query.
- A cancelled or superseded fetch no longer writes anything. Resetting a query before its fetch starts leaves it idle (and `use_is_fetching` drops back to zero), a response racing `cancel_queries` no longer overwrites an optimistic update, and an older response can no longer overwrite a newer one.
- Data written with `set_query_data`, `set_query_data_at`, or `update_query_data` is garbage collected after its gc time like any other unobserved query, so writes now start a timer task on the executor. A query keeps at most one cleanup timer, a stale timer can no longer evict the query that replaced it, and native hosts without a tokio runtime share one timer thread instead of starting a thread per sleep.
- Checking whether queries are active no longer subscribes the caller to every observer's `enabled` closure.

Cache identity is now explicit:

- An unnamed `QueryScope` or `InfiniteQueryScope` whose fetcher closure captures values panics on first use, rather than sharing one cache with every scope built from the same closure. Name it with `.with_name(..)`.
- Key hashes and named scope ids are stable across platforms and Rust releases (`usize` and lengths hash as 64-bit), so a server's dehydrated cache matches the browser's. `QueryClient::dehydrate` panics for an unnamed scope, whose id differs between binaries. Keys whose hashes collide are compared for equality and stay separate queries.

`InfiniteQueryScope` builders no longer change clones made earlier, and gain `with_retry_delay` and `with_data_eq`. The docs now say that hydrated data refetches in the background unless its scope has a stale time, and the optimistic update recipe cancels in-flight fetches and removes the optimistic entry when there was nothing to roll back to.

In `leptoskit_use`, `signal_debounced` and `signal_throttled` no longer notify subscribers when a write leaves the value unchanged.

changesets.summary: Route every URL and every file name safely
changesets.details:
`Route::parse` now reads URLs the way a browser does, so it never fails: a stray `%` stays as it is, escapes that aren't UTF-8 become U+FFFD, and `.` and `..` segments are resolved. `Navigation::from_browser()` mounts on any URL, and `ParseError` and `UrlError` are gone; `parse` and `from_browser` return `NoMatch`. Only path values decide whether a route matches: a query value that doesn't parse is ignored, so `/notes/42?highlight=x` is note 42, and a path parameter never reads from the query, so `/about?lang=fr` has no language.

An href never holds an empty, `.` or `..` segment and never starts with `//`: an optional segment holding one is left out, and a required segment or catch-all value holding one ends the path, so an empty value can no longer produce a link to another site.

The generator turns every file name into valid Rust, escaping modules and variants the same way (`404.rs` is `_404`, `self.rs` is `self_` and `Self_`, `gen.rs` is `gen_`), and reports a problem it cannot fix instead of panicking. A route with optional segments is ordered once for each combination of them present and absent, so `/about` reaches `[[lang]]/about.rs` before `[section].rs`, and two routes that match the same URLs through their optional segments are reported. A `_layout.rs` without a `layout` is an error, private helpers named like exports are ignored, `home.ios.rs` and the other `platform_module!` suffixes are recognised as platform overrides, and route struct fields are classified exactly as `#[derive(Route)]` reads them.

changesets.summary: Add job steps, cron, actions, and an inbox
changesets.details:
Background jobs gain everything slow, unreliable work needs: `cx.step(…)` saves each step's result so a retry resumes where the last attempt stopped, `cx.key()` gives outside calls an idempotency key that is the same on every attempt, `cx.mutate(…)` applies a mutation once per job and step, and `rpc::Error::retry` and `rpc::Error::permanent` say whether to try again. `#[rpc::job]` takes `queue`, `retries`, `backoff = exponential(…)`, `deadline`, `timeout`, `serialize_by`, `visible_to`, and `on_failure`; queues have a concurrency that holds across servers, configured in `[rpc.jobs]`. `#[rpc::cron("…")]` enqueues a job once per tick however many servers run. Jobs report progress, can be cancelled, are visible only to whoever enqueued them, and wake workers the moment they are enqueued. `use_job` follows a job live over the socket.

`#[rpc::action]` declares work someone waits for that may call anything: it runs as the caller, outside any transaction, is never retried, and is called over `POST /api/<name>`, from generated clients, and with `use_action`.

`cx.notify(account, notice)` puts a notice in a person's inbox from a mutation, a job, or an action, and `use_inbox()` shows it on every device they have open, with an unread count, `mark_read`, and `mark_all_read`.

changesets.summary: One live hub, server-sent events, and exact versions
changesets.details:
A server now reads the database's change log once for every connection, and the live connection works where a WebSocket can't.

- **One hub per server.** `rpc::server::Live` reads each commit once, finds the subscriptions it could change through an index by table, and re-runs only those. Subscriptions to the same query with the same arguments by the same caller share one re-run and one diff, on any number of connections. Each connection receives one transition per batch of commits. `LiveStats` gains `commits` (read once each) and `resumes`.
- **Server-sent events.** `GET /live/events` streams the same frames as server-sent events, with each transition's version as its event id, and `POST /live/frames?connection=<id>` takes the client's frames. Both are authenticated like the socket, and a post must come from the stream's caller. `Last-Event-ID` resumes. The browser client switches to them after two failed WebSocket upgrades; native apps stay on the WebSocket.
- **Read-your-writes from the commit itself.** A mutation's `done.version` is the version its commit took in the change log, from the new `Tx::commit_version()`. Every transition names the version it reflects, and a connection waiting for a version that changed none of its results gets an empty transition, so mutations never hang. `LiveClient::mutate`, `LiveClient::act`, `use_live_mutation` and `use_live_action` resolve once the client has applied that version.
- **Actions over the connection.** The new `act` frame runs an `#[rpc::action]` with the same identity and errors as `POST /api/<name>`.
- **Resume.** `hello { resume: { version, queries } }` subscribes again without a full reload: the server sends only the results that changed since `version`, or everything when the log was pruned past it. The client keeps its last applied version and resumes after a reconnect or a drain.
- **`leptoskit_db`.** `Tx::commit_version()`, `ChangeLog::next_ready()` and `Context::is_empty()`.

changesets.summary: Live queries over a WebSocket
changesets.details:
`leptoskit_rpc` gains the live side of its operations, on top of the database's live invalidation feed.

- **`rpc::server::Live`.** `GET /live` speaks `leptoskit.live.v1.json`: subscribe to registered queries by name, run mutations on the same socket, and receive what changed. It identifies callers with the same `rpc::Identify` implementation the HTTP routes use, checks the upgrade's `Origin`, re-runs queries as the caller, and sends only results that changed. `Server::live()` builds one from an existing server, and `Live::drain()` reconnects every socket with jitter for a deployment.
- **Keyed patches.** A list of rows with an `id` travels as removals and positioned upserts; everything else travels whole. A slow connection gets the latest state whole instead of every intermediate step.
- **Limits.** 256 subscriptions per connection, 512 KiB per result, and 1 MiB per frame, enforced before a query can grow the server without bound.
- **`rpc::use_live`.** The screen-facing hook is `use_rpc_query` plus a subscription: the first value comes from the ordinary client (HTTP, or in process while rendering), and updates are written into the same `leptoskit_query` cache, so suspense, SSR, hydration and devtools work unchanged. The client reconnects with backoff, resubscribes, and re-sends pending mutations with their idempotency keys.
- **Transports.** The browser uses `leptoskit_plugin_websocket`'s browser client; a native guest uses its guest client. Without either, `use_live` is exactly `use_rpc_query`.
- **Facade.** `leptoskit` gains `rpc-live`.
- **Docs.** "Real-time screens" covers opting tables in, serving the socket, watching a query, what arrives, reconnecting, and the limits.

changesets.summary: Streams, pinned pages, an offline queue, and re-auth
changesets.details:
The live connection now carries streams and long lists, keeps working through a dropped network, and follows sign-in without a reload.

- **Streams.** `#[rpc::stream]` declares an `async fn` that returns `impl Stream<Item = T>` (or `Item = rpc::Result<T>`), runs as the caller, and implements the new `rpc::StreamOperation`. The client opens it with `stream { stream, name, args, credits }`, grants more room with `credit { stream, n }`, and stops it with `cancel { stream }`. The server reads the next item only once it has a credit, so a slow client never makes it buffer more than it asked for. A stream ends with `end { stream, reason, err? }`: `done`, `failed` or `interrupted`. `#[rpc::stream(resumable)]` takes a `cursor` argument, its items implement `rpc::Resumable`, and the client opens it again from the last item's cursor after a reconnect. `rpc::use_stream(move || S { … })` shows one on screen. Streams work over the WebSocket and server-sent events, and `#[api]` publishes them as the new `Kind::Stream` and `ApiKind::Stream`, in `/asyncapi.json` and not in `/openapi.json`. Generated SDKs skip them for now.
- **Pinned pages.** A query that takes `rpc::PageArgs` and returns `rpc::Page<T>` implements `rpc::Paginated`, and `rpc::paginate(db, query, &page, order, key)` reads one page by a unique column. `rpc::use_live_paginated(move |page| Q { …, page }, size)` builds on `leptoskit_query`'s infinite queries, with `.load_more()` and `.has_more()`. Every loaded page is its own live subscription, and loading more pins the last page at its end, so an insert into page one lengthens it and leaves page two alone. A page's rows travel as a patch of its `items`.
- **The offline queue.** Mutations and actions dispatched while the live connection is down wait in order and go out when it comes back. `ClientConfig::offline_queue(true)` also keeps them on the device (`localStorage` in the browser, the store plugin in a native app), so they replay after a restart: mutations with their idempotency key, and actions only if they were never sent. `ClientConfig::offline_store` takes any `QueueStore`, such as a `MemoryQueue`. `rpc::use_live_status()` reports the connection's state and how many calls wait.
- **Re-authenticating an open connection.** `rpc::client::reauthenticate()` has the live connection read as the current credentials: a bearer token goes in an `auth` frame on the open connection, and a cookie session reconnects without resuming. `leptoskit_auth`'s client calls it on every sign-in, sign-out and token renewal, with its `rpc` feature on.
- **Read-your-writes from the ordinary hook.** `use_mutation(mutation_scope::<M>())` goes over the live connection while it is open, and resolves once its writes are on screen, as `use_live_mutation` does; otherwise it calls over HTTP.
- **A fix for keyed patches.** A row inserted before others in a keyed list now goes in at its place on the client, instead of replacing the row there.
- **Testing.** `rpc::testing::LiveClients` connects real `LiveClient`s to a `Live` in the same process, with headers to sign in by and an `outage` switch.
